outcome: Nothing has settled the problem since 26 January 2024: no composite n with φ(n) | n − 1 has been found or excluded, and every source read as of 13 October 2026 still treats it as open. The in-window events are a June 2026 preprint (Kominers) proving conditional lower bounds on the multiplicative order of φ(n) mod n for a hypothetical counterexample, a June 2026 expository note that claims no result, and 2024–2026 work on spoof and unitary variants of the equation.
problem_asks: One question: does there exist a composite integer n ≥ 2 with φ(n) dividing n − 1? Equivalently, is the implication 'φ(n) | n − 1 implies n is prime' true for every n ≥ 2? The converse is trivial (for prime p, φ(p) = p − 1), so the open content is the non-existence of composite solutions. The statement asks for no bound, count, size or structure of any counterexample. The composite reading is needed because n = 1 satisfies φ(1) | 0 without being prime; the Wikipedia lead reads the problem over composite n.

events.what_happened: D. H. Lehmer posed the question in 1932 (On Euler's totient function, Bull. AMS 38) and showed that any composite solution must be odd, squarefree, have at least 7 distinct prime factors, and be a Carmichael number. Read from the Wikipedia article's history section; the 1932 paper itself was not opened.
events.delivers: Restricts any composite solution to be odd, squarefree, Carmichael, with ω(n) ≥ 7. Establishes no existence or non-existence.
events.remains: Existence of any composite n with φ(n) | n − 1 (the whole problem).

events.what_happened: T. Yamada, 'On Lehmer's problem and related problems' (arXiv:2303.16853, submitted 29 Mar 2023). Covers both signs; the N − 1 case is the Lehmer equation with index M. The abstract does not state whether Lehmer's problem is open.

events.what_happened: S. D. Kominers, 'Effective lower bounds for the multiplicative order of φ(n) modulo a Lehmer counterexample' (PDF dated 6 June 2026, hosted on the author's website; no arXiv or journal version found). For a hypothetical counterexample n, with h = ord_n(φ(n)) and a = (n − 1)/φ(n): Thm 1.1 gives h ≥ 41 if ω(n) ≥ 15, and h ≥ 8249 if ω(n) ≥ 1991. The first hypothesis holds for every counterexample by Renze (2004, unrefereed notebook); the second holds whenever a ≥ 3 (Grytczuk–Wójtowicz). Method: the congruence φ(n) ≡ −a − 1 (mod n) with a sharp product bound for a. Presented as a quantification of a Deaconescu remark (h ≥ 5). The footnote on the author line says: 'I used LLMs to assist with coding, computations, and analysis in the preparation of this article, particularly GPT-5.5 Pro and Claude 4.7 Opus (accessed in part via Poe with the support of Quora, where I am an advisor).' and 'The problem, methods, and eventual written form are my own; and of course any errors remain my responsibility.' disputes.summary: Current best prime-factor bound: ω(n) ≥ 14 (Cohen–Hagis 1980, per Wikipedia, MathWorld and Burcsi et al.) versus ω(n) ≥ 15 (Renze 2004 notebook, per Burcsi et al., Kominers 2026 and a Yamada excerpt). MathWorld attributes d(n) ≥ 14 and n > 10^22 to Pinch via a Carmichael table; Burcsi credits Pinch with N > 10^30.

Size bound on any counterexample is reported as 10^20 (Cohen–Hagis, Wikipedia; OEIS A213514), 10^22 (MathWorld via Pinch; Renze notebook page quoting Cohen–Hagis), 10^26 (Renze, per secondary sources), 10^28 (Pinch abstract, search excerpt) and 10^30 (Pinch poster, search excerpt; Burcsi et al.).
Whether a ≥ 3 (a = (n−1)/φ(n)) holds for every counterexample: Norman (2021) claims k ≥ 3 for every k with kφ(n) = n − 1; Kominers (2026) says it is not known. Not reconciled in any source read.

Four claimed proofs or partial results were withdrawn or are unverified: Pourgholi (2015, both preprints withdrawn as incomplete); Sabihi (2016, no withdrawal, no verification found); Xiao (2017, withdrawn 2019, comment 'error in Theorem 2.3'); Zriaa (2023, withdrawn Dec 2023, comment 'error in Theorem 2.3'). None is accepted in any source read, and the 2026 sources read still treat the problem as open.
Hagis (1988) case 3 | n bound (ω ≥ 298848, n > 10^1937042) appears with garbled exponents in every secondary source; the original was not read.
Molnar–Singh arXiv title ('Positive spoof Lehmer factorizations') differs from the Integers title ('Spoof Lehmer Factorizations'); same paper.

summary: Nothing has settled the problem since 26 January 2024. The one open part of the statement, whether any composite n ≥ 2 has φ(n) | n − 1, is still open on every source read, including the Molnar–Singh paper (Integers, February 2026), which says the problem has been 'attacked repeatedly in the ensuing century', and Kominers (June 2026). No counterexample is known, and the only exhaustive exclusion is Pinch's computation (2006, excerpt-only), which rules out solutions below 10^28 or 10^30 depending on the source. The in-window events are: (1) Kominers, 6 June 2026, a preprint (author's website only; no arXiv or journal version found) proving that for a hypothetical counterexample the order of φ(n) mod n is at least 41 if ω(n) ≥ 15 and at least 8249 if ω(n) ≥ 1991, the latter requiring a ≥ 3. Its first bound rests on Renze's 2004 notebook, whose page I read states no bound. Its footnote says 'I used LLMs to assist with coding, computations, and analysis … particularly GPT-5.5 Pro and Claude 4.7 Opus', and that 'The problem, methods, and eventual written form are my own'; I read this footnote through a text-extraction proxy. No review, comment or citing paper was found by 13 October 2026. (2) A Zenodo expository note (20 June 2026) that claims no proof. (3) Spoof, unitary and Deaconescu variants (Molnar–Singh 2024/2026, Hasanalizade 2026, Mandal 2025), all different equations and discounted. The pre-window record is a chain of partial bounds (Lehmer 1932; Cohen–Hagis 1980; Lieuwens 1970; Kishore 1977; Wall 1980; Hagis 1988; Grytczuk–Wójtowicz 2003; Luca–Pomerance 2011; Burcsi et al. 2011; Renze 2004; Pinch 2006; Burek–Żmija 2018; Yamada 2023) and four withdrawn or unverified claimed proofs (Pourgholi 2015, Sabihi 2016, Xiao 2017, Zriaa 2023). Where the call is close: the Kominers result is a conditional constraint on a hypothetical object, not a bound on a quantity the problem names, so it could be read as progress on the problem or as no progress; the AI footnote names two systems but gives no step, so whether either contributed load-bearing mathematics cannot be determined from the text, and I have recorded both systems in ai.systems with the authors' quote for the later pass to weigh. Among the AI-involved items I found, the Verhoeff result (IO+, 9 October 2026) concerns Lehmer's permutation conjecture, a namesake, and its systems are not recorded here because they bear on a different problem and the account is press coverage. Several AI and AI-adjacent searches (GPT-5.5 Pro, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini, AlphaEvolve, the Erdős problem database, formal-conjectures) found no AI result on this problem. Caveats: the pre-window bounds were read from secondary excerpts unless noted; full texts of Sabihi 2016, Norman 2021, Molnar–Singh 2024 and Hasanalizade 2026 were not read, so their AI and checking fields reflect the abstract and theorem statements only.
competing_reading: Read the Kominers preprint as progress with a plausible AI contribution: it is the only in-window item that moves a quantity (the order of φ(n) mod n; lower bounds on ω(n) for a counterexample), its authors name GPT-5.5 Pro and Claude 4.7 Opus as doing 'analysis' and 'computations', and the 8249 bound uses a ≥ 3, which Norman (2021) claims is always true. Read it instead as no progress on the problem and no load-bearing AI: the bounds constrain only a hypothetical object, the problem's own question (existence) is untouched, the authors state that the problem and methods are theirs, and the AI sentence is a general disclosure that names no step.
what_would_settle_it: (a) A journal or arXiv version of Kominers (2026) with a step-level contribution statement, and whether the 'computations' include an LLM-written verification. (b) The output of Renze's 2004 notebook (LehmerArticle.nb, MathSource 5483) showing ω ≥ 15, and the Pinch 2006 paper with its stated size bound. (c) A reconciliation between Norman (2021, k ≥ 3 always) and Kominers (2026, a ≥ 3 'not known'), either by a published check of Norman or by a correction. (d) A published review, erratum or withdrawal for Sabihi (2016), or any later paper that cites or refutes it. (e) Any post-June-2026 paper that cites Kominers, or a later paper that still calls the problem open without citing it.

judgement.why: The statement asks only whether a composite n with φ(n) | n−1 exists. Restrictions on a hypothetical counterexample (prime-factor counts, size bounds, counting bounds, index bounds, Kominers' order bounds) move quantities while the question stays open, so they are scored bound. Pinch's exclusion below 10^28/10^30 is a finite search, so instances. The function-field, number-field, +1, spoof, unitary and Deaconescu papers and the two Lehmer namesakes answer different questions: variant. The withdrawn claims are knocked_down. Sabihi's unwithdrawn whole claim is not_credible: it combines a landmark claim, an author with no located record in the field, ten years without uptake, and later papers still calling the problem open. The close call is Kominers 2026: it is a conditional constraint and could be read as none, but it proves an unconditional-given-ω≥15 lower bound on a quantity attached to any counterexample, the same kind of result as the classical ω bounds, so bound. Its AI disclosure says LLMs assisted with 'coding, computations, and analysis' while 'the problem, methods, and eventual written form are my own'; that names no mathematical step produced by a model, so ai_role none.
judgement.doubts: Kominers' AI footnote is vague; if a later version showed a model produced a bounding argument, the role would be assisted. The Kominers first bound leans on Renze's unrefereed ω ≥ 15. Pre-snapshot journal verifications rest on secondary reports of publication.
